comments.content: This is not regarding a 'health check' which is what you are referring to. Eresdev could explain better but it's that the RPC provider might be a bad actor and our RPC requests can be used to hijack the card feature.

I love this approach actually because if we ever return the Ubiquity RPCs that once were then they could live here too as they'd be the most trusted
It's unclear to me whether we are supporting all networks with cards right off the bat or if you intend on releasing chains gradually, if so this sounds good but personally I'd prefer the new function as it sounds more useful and re-useable. You could pass the whitelist from the ui logic into the handler instead of constantly updating the handler pkg with new rpcs.

@rndquu How long would you estimate this task to take and considering the severity of the tenderly fork situation which we both know is dangerous for more than just cards, I'm assuming that the priority just increased for this task too?
Happy to get a start on things if I'm allowed to carry out the task.

@EresDev has made it known it's possible for pay.ubq.fi' new card feature to be taken over/hijacked by an RPC provider if it turns out they are nefarious.
```ts
const chains = await fetcher("https://chainid.network/chains.json");
const chainTvls = await fetcher("https://api.llama.fi/chains");
```
This is how chainlist fetch their RPC list which we also use, they validate chains based on DeFiLlama TVL stats.
Their UI produces a "Score" value but I don't think that's something we can use to determine a level of trust and I think it may be UI specific as there's nothing like that returned from in this [json](https://chainid.network/chains.json)
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6048509f-9d40-4787-8092-46d62d2d7a08)
Problems:
1. Using a service like Alchemy or Infura drastically decreases the number of networks that we can support
2. Services like above have a service/subscription fee normally and we avoid that at all costs.
3. I'm not aware of any other free service or service provider that fills our need here.
Solutions:
1. general whitelist - not scalable, requires manual validation across hundreds of networks.
2. [service provider](https://www.alchemy.com/best/rpc-node-providers) - solves the trust issues but involves costs and limits our offering.
3. specific whitelist - cards I think are limited to our designated chains, if so, we could build a specific whitelist for those chains and only use that list for the card feature logic.
I was contacted on TG a while back with a shill for this https://github.com/erpc/erpc, which is our `rpc-handler` on steroids by the looks of it, idk if we are considering just replacing this package completely in place of a 3rd party offering, are we?
_original [context](https://github.com/ubiquity/pay.ubq.fi/pull/345#discussion_r1811910326)_

comments.content:
I mean dangerous in the sense that we will ask potentially 10+ providers to execute this transaction for us and return the response. 
If a user is not aware and puts a token transfer through for example then it would execute n times wouldn't it? 
What they probably meant to do was transfer through the `provider` and verify the `txHash` with `consensusCall`.
Ahh yeah I understand my confusion now, I appreciate the feedback.

I debated this myself a little.
I went with `JSON.Stringify` at first and then return returning `JSON.parse` but some response data is enormous so I went with `hash` instead thinking it was more universal than what you've pointed it out to be.
Other than `JSON.Stringify` I'm not sure how we can match responses with certainty across all methods/request results.

Yeah it increments each time a response is the same. 
In this logic we were matching the hash, but as you've highlighted that needs changed to something more generic.

what about `.hash ?? .transactionHash` I feel that might be better but still a lot of methods would be excluded.
Perhaps `consensusCall` takes a a 3rd param which is the prop of the return data that we need to compare and then allow the user to tell us?

I've implemented `.hash ?? .transactionHash` for now as that covers `eth_getTransactionReceipt` at least.
A 3rd param sounds scalable across all `eth_` methods, failing that, stringifying the results might be the best bet.
The test would be deterministic because if the function is successful it will return a valid response object which I assert props of in the new e2e tests. I think that is sufficient enough but lmk

Usually we mock all API responses but I built the tests specifically so that we mocked as little as possible which is why we have a local `Anvil` instance for write ops and use the real public nodes in other tests. 
I think typically you shouldn't use the real responses but I felt it was a better way to test this package so I wasn't potentially fooling myself. 
Nock was quick and easy with little overhead and because it's only used for one test suite I didn't think it would be too much of an issue.
`rpcHandler.security.consensusCall` is now in place

Addressed this as best I could mate. I couldn't think of how to handle the conditional without a string or prop comparison  but I refactored into a cleaner format.
I'm hoping for a task specifically for refactoring, written by myself or someone else, but I'll make small adjustments as PRs go through regardless.
It should be resolved now thank you for pointing that out

So the trouble with using the entire response object is that they are not 100% consistent across all providers. So we sort all props and sub props of the response and then stringify but this isn't foolproof because even then providers inject additional data that others don't.
One example I've seen is `author` being present in some `getBlockByNumber` while not in others but I'm not sure how big of an issue this is exactly.
I think this is reasonable for V1 but if it struggles for this reason I think 3rd param might be the way forward.

@EresDev I'm confused now because the purpose of the scripts and subsequently these tests were to test the build, the final `/dist` output that is consumed by package installers. The unit tests all import from `/types`, between the two the only difference of what's being tested was the fact it was `/dist` imports.

`eth_getBlockByNumber` is the method being tested which uses `latest` to obtain the latest block. We don't necessarily need to verify a block number, just that it returns a valid `block` response?
By my understanding, the method is deterministic in two ways: 1. it throws 2. it returns a response object for the method - which is verified with the prop asserts always present in the `block` object. 
Should we hardcode a specific block number and compare the exact response object with a manually fetched `block`, is this what you mean?

comments.content:
If `pay.ubq.fi` uses a malicious RPC node then its owner is able to generate tons of gift cards orders using fake tx hashes because [here](https://github.com/ubiquity/pay.ubq.fi/blob/e5555984e839717f3cf0ae82c39d136c89044bd0/functions/post-order.ts#L47) tx receipt would be retrieved exactly from a malicious RPC.
Chances are slim.
I suppose the safest option is to finally run a [private](https://developers.cloudflare.com/web3/ethereum-gateway/) node and use https://github.com/ubiquity/rpc-handler as a fallback.

Whitelisting a public "official" node or even a private node (deployed via smth like https://chainstack.com/protocols/gnosis-chain/) doesn't solve the issue when RPC node becomes malicious.
Here are 2 issues actually:
1. We need a list of stable RPC nodes (which is some cases not the fastest RPC node in a list from https://chainlist.org/). So perhaps it makes sense (as @EresDev proposed) to have a new class `RpcHandlerOfficial` which would offer a list of 2-3 stable RPCs. It will be our job to manually maintain that list.
2. On the `pay.ubq.fi` [backend](https://github.com/ubiquity/pay.ubq.fi/tree/e5555984e839717f3cf0ae82c39d136c89044bd0/functions) side we can't really trust any RPC node (unless it's a private RPC node hosted on our side). We could introduce a simple consensus check, like if tx receipt exists at least in 2 RPC nodes then there's nothing malicious. This is kind of a overoptimization looking at the current "mint gift card" feature state but it'd good not to forget the issue exists.

In the context of the `pay.ubq.fi` backend we don't need to write anything on-chain, we just need to check that 2 separate RPC nodes return the same [txReceipt](https://github.com/ubiquity/pay.ubq.fi/blob/e5555984e839717f3cf0ae82c39d136c89044bd0/functions/post-order.ts#L47) for the provided [txHash](https://github.com/ubiquity/pay.ubq.fi/blob/e5555984e839717f3cf0ae82c39d136c89044bd0/functions/post-order.ts#L42).

To sum up, as a part of this issue we could add a new method `consensusCall(rpcMethod, params, minimumConsensusAmount)` which would:
1. Create `minimumConsensusAmount` instances of separate RPC nodes
2. Call `rpcMethod(params)` on all of the nodes from step 1
3. Return the result only if it's the same on all nodes
In the end [here](https://github.com/ubiquity/pay.ubq.fi/blob/e5555984e839717f3cf0ae82c39d136c89044bd0/functions/post-order.ts#L47) we should be able to call smth like `consensusCall("getTransactionReceipt", txHash, 2)` to make sure the tx receipt is the same in a couple of RPC nodes.
P.S. The `consensusCall()` method seems to be read-only
